anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-layer SQL or transactional design forces the engine to scan or manipulate far more data than the business logic really needs, resulting in excessive row touch, long-running statements, and bloated transactions.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, so index look-ups, page links, or key orders no longer reliably reflect the true contents of the tables.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage subsystem cannot sustain the read/write volume demanded by the database, driving queue depths and latency beyond acceptable thresholds.

When all three conditions coexist, the system exhibits extreme and erratic slowdown: heavy, non-selective queries and long transactions repeatedly fall back from damaged indexes to full table scans, flooding the I/O subsystem with random and sequential reads that it is already unable to serve. Checksum or page-verification errors intermingle with surging I/O wait events, slow-query logs balloon, retry storms appear at the application tier, and recovery or consistency checks become protracted or fail outright. Administrators observe widening latency variance, unexplained row discrepancies between index and heap probes, sporadic corruption errors, and storage devices stuck at 100 % utilization even when CPU usage is modest.

Causally, poorly written SQL magnifies the read and write pressure on both indexes and data pages, accelerating wear on suspect blocks and increasing the likelihood of surfaces interactions with latent corruptions. Each corruption encountered can force the optimizer to abandon otherwise efficient access paths, switching to full scans that multiply I/O volume. The resulting surge of physical I/O exacerbates an already saturated storage layer, further lengthening service times and inflating in-flight I/O queues. Prolonged latency keeps transactions open longer, intensifying contention and the window during which additional corruptions or write-back failures may occur. In turn, extended storage stalls heighten the risk of incomplete writes or torn pages, feeding back into the integrity problem and creating a self-reinforcing spiral of degradation that is difficult to isolate to any single layer.

entry.official_definition: Sets the interval between optional checks that the client is still connected while running queries.
entry.trigger_condition: During a long-running query, PostgreSQL polls the socket at this interval and can detect a closed connection sooner.
entry.workload_impact: Long-running queries can be aborted sooner after the kernel reports that the client connection is closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, disabling connection checks.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
